title: Reproductive System
tagline: Male and female reproductive systems, the menstrual cycle, methods of birth control and reproductive health.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Human reproduction is internal and viviparous: sperm fertilises the ovum in the fallopian tube and the embryo implants in the uterus, nourished until birth. This chapter covers the male and female reproductive systems and their glandular contributions, the hormonal control of the approximately 28-day menstrual cycle with its ovarian and uterine phases, and the principles behind birth control methods — barrier, hormonal, surgical, chemical and natural — together with reproductive health topics including sexually transmitted infections and the value of contraception in family planning. Understanding hormone timing explains both fertility and how each contraceptive method works.

facts.label: Menstrual cycle
facts.value: ~28 days; ovulation around day 14; controlled by FSH, LH, oestrogen, progesterone

facts.label: Fertilisation
facts.value: Occurs in the fallopian tube; implantation in the uterus about 6–7 days later

facts.label: Contraception
facts.value: Barrier, hormonal, surgical, chemical and natural methods

blocks.text: The male system produces sperm in the testes, which lie outside the body in the scrotum because spermatogenesis needs a temperature slightly below body temperature. Testosterone from interstitial cells drives sperm production and secondary sexual characters. Sperm mature and are nourished by fluid from the seminal vesicles and prostate gland; the mixed semen travels through the vas deferens, joins the urethra, and passes out through the penis. The female system pairs two ovaries, which produce ova and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone, with the uterus where an embryo implants and develops. Each month an ovulated egg enters a fallopian tube — the normal site of fertilisation — and travels to the uterus lined by the endometrium, a layer thickened in preparation for implantation. Fertilisation typically occurs in the upper third of the fallopian tube; the zygote divides as it travels, implants about six to seven days later, and pregnancy hormones then prevent menstruation so the endometrium is maintained throughout gestation.

items.meaning: Male gonads producing sperm and testosterone; held in the scrotum for temperature control.
Female gonad producing ova, oestrogen and progesterone.
Uterine lining that thickens monthly and is shed during menstruation if unfertilised.
Fusion of sperm and ovum, normally in the fallopian tube.
Attachment of the blastocyst to the endometrium about a week after fertilisation.
Male sex hormone driving sperm production and secondary sexual characters.

items: Scrotum keeps testes ~2–3 °C below body temperature — essential for viable sperm.
Seminiferous tubules make sperm; interstitial (Leydig) cells make testosterone.
Seminal vesicles + prostate add alkaline, sugar-rich fluid to form semen.
Ovaries release one ovum roughly monthly; ovulation usually occurs around day 14.
Fallopian tube with ciliated lining sweeps the ovum toward the uterus — the fertilisation site.
Endometrium thickens under oestrogen/progesterone; if no implantation occurs it breaks down — menstruation.
Fertilisation -> zygote -> morula -> blastocyst -> implantation in the uterus.

items.text: Ectopic pregnancy: an embryo implants in the fallopian tube instead of the uterus — a medical emergency.
items.note: Confirms why peristalsis/cilia of the tube must carry the embryo to the uterus.

items.text: Testosterone at puberty causes deeper voice, facial hair and muscle growth — secondary sexual characters.
items.note: The same hormone drives spermatogenesis, linking the two male functions.

learn.title: The menstrual cycle and its hormonal control

blocks.text: The menstrual cycle averages about 28 days and has four phases. Menstruation (days 1–5): with fertilisation absent, progesterone and oestrogen fall, the endometrium breaks down and is shed. Follicular phase (days 1–13): the pituitary's FSH stimulates follicles in the ovary to develop, one becoming dominant; growing follicles secrete oestrogen, which rebuilds and thickens the endometrium. Ovulation (about day 14): a surge of LH triggers the release of the secondary oocyte from the ruptured follicle. Luteal phase (days 15–28): the collapsed follicle becomes the corpus luteum, secreting progesterone which maintains the secretory endometrium, inhibits further FSH/LH so no new follicle matures, and prepares the lining for implantation. If fertilisation does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone and oestrogen plunge, and menstruation begins the next cycle. If pregnancy occurs, the implanted embryo secretes hCG which maintains the corpus luteum, progesterone stays high, and menstruation does not occur — which is why hCG is the hormone detected in pregnancy tests.

items: Days 1–5: menstruation — endometrium shed as progesterone falls.
Days 1–13: FSH develops follicles; oestrogen rebuilds the endometrium.
Day 14: LH surge causes ovulation — release of the secondary oocyte.
Days 15–28: corpus luteum secretes progesterone maintaining the thick secretory endometrium.
Progesterone inhibits FSH and LH — no new follicle matures during the luteal phase.
No fertilisation -> corpus luteum degenerates -> hormones fall -> menstruation.
Pregnancy -> embryo makes hCG -> corpus luteum maintained -> progesterone stays high -> no menstruation.

items.meaning: Luteinising hormone; its surge triggers ovulation and maintains the corpus luteum.
Luteal hormone maintaining the endometrium and inhibiting FSH/LH.
Hormone from the implanted embryo maintaining the corpus luteum; detected in pregnancy tests.
Release of the ovum from the ovary, around day 14.

items.text: A missed period can indicate pregnancy within days because hCG keeps progesterone high.
items.note: The same corpus luteum support that would otherwise collapse at day ~28.

items.text: Stress or extreme weight loss can stop menstruation — the hypothalamus-pituitary signalling is disrupted.
items.note: Shows the cycle's dependence on hormonal signalling, not just the ovaries.

blocks.text: Contraceptive methods prevent pregnancy by blocking sperm from meeting the ovum, preventing ovulation, or stopping implantation. Barrier methods — condoms (male and female) — physically block sperm and have the added advantage of reducing sexually transmitted infection transmission. Hormonal methods (combined pills, patches, injections) use oestrogen and progesterone to inhibit FSH and LH, preventing ovulation; they are highly effective when used correctly but do not protect against STIs. Intrauterine devices are placed in the uterus and alter the uterine environment, preventing implantation or sperm survival. Chemical methods use spermicidal jellies to immobilise sperm, usually with a barrier. Surgical methods are permanent: vasectomy cuts the vas deferens, blocking sperm from the semen, while tubal ligation blocks the fallopian tubes; both are irreversible and used by couples who have completed their families. Natural methods include the rhythm (safe period) method — avoiding intercourse near ovulation — and withdrawal; both depend on precise cycle knowledge and have high failure rates. Reproductive health also includes awareness of sexually transmitted infections such as HIV/AIDS and gonorrhoea, prevention through barrier use and single partners, and family planning for maternal and child wellbeing.

items: Barrier: condoms block sperm AND reduce STI transmission — the only method with both benefits.
Hormonal: pills/injections inhibit FSH/LH so no ovulation occurs; high effectiveness with correct use.
IUD: placed in uterus; prevents implantation or kills sperm.
Chemical: spermicides immobilise sperm — usually combined with a barrier.
Surgical: vasectomy (male) / tubal ligation (female) — permanent, near-100% effective.
Natural: rhythm method avoids fertile days (around ovulation); withdrawal — both high failure rates.
STIs spread by bodily fluids; condoms reduce risk; HIV has no cure — prevention is central.
Family planning protects maternal and child health by spacing pregnancies.

items.text: The combined pill works by masking the cycle's hormone signals so the pituitary never triggers ovulation.
items.note: If pills are missed, FSH/LH can recover and ovulation may occur — hence strict dosing.

items.text: Condom use doubles as STI protection — the key public-health point in exam answers on reproductive health.
items.note: Barrier methods are the only contraception that also reduces infection spread.

keyPoints: Testes produce sperm and testosterone; the scrotum keeps them below body temperature.
Ovaries produce ova, oestrogen and progesterone; ovulation is around day 14.
Fertilisation occurs in the fallopian tube; implantation in the uterus about a week later.
Menstrual cycle: menstruation → follicular phase → ovulation → luteal phase.
FSH develops follicles; LH surge triggers ovulation; progesterone maintains the endometrium.
Without fertilisation the corpus luteum degenerates and menstruation follows; with pregnancy hCG maintains it.
Contraception blocks sperm, prevents ovulation, or prevents implantation.
Condoms are the only method that also reduces STI transmission.
Hormonal methods inhibit FSH/LH; surgical methods are permanent; natural methods have high failure rates.
experimentFocus: Cycle-charting questions: given 'day X', identify which hormones are high, the ovarian state and the endometrial state — practise day 5 vs day 14 vs day 25.
Pregnancy-test reasoning: hCG comes from the implanted embryo, not the ovary — its presence explains a positive test.
Contraceptive mechanism answers must state WHERE each method acts (block sperm at cervix, stop ovulation at pituitary, prevent implantation in uterus).
examFocus: Menstrual cycle questions demand hormone names with functions — FSH, LH, oestrogen, progesterone — not just the phase names.
Name the site of fertilisation (fallopian tube) and implantation (uterus/endometrium) explicitly.
Birth control: give at least one example per category with its mechanism; mention STI protection when discussing condoms.
Reproductive health answers should mention STI transmission routes and prevention — condoms, single partner, screening.

vocabulary.meaning: Monthly cycle of hormonal and uterine changes preparing for pregnancy.
Release of a mature ovum from the ovary.
Uterine lining that thickens and is shed each cycle.
Sexually transmitted infection, e.g. HIV, gonorrhoea.

questions.prompt: The normal site of fertilisation in the human female is the:
questions.explanation: The ovum meets sperm in the fallopian tube; the ciliated lining then sweeps the zygote toward the uterus for implantation.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the uterus — that is where implantation occurs, not fertilisation.

questions.prompt: Which hormone surge triggers ovulation around day 14 of the menstrual cycle?
questions.explanation: A sharp surge of luteinising hormone ruptures the mature follicle and releases the secondary oocyte.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing FSH — it develops the follicle, but LH causes its rupture.

questions.prompt: Which contraceptive method also reduces the transmission of sexually transmitted infections?
questions.explanation: The condom is a barrier physically preventing sperm and also blocking the exchange of bodily fluids through which STIs spread.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the pill — hormonal methods prevent ovulation but offer no infection protection.

questions.prompt: The function of progesterone during the luteal phase is to:
options: Stimulate FSH to develop a new follicle
Maintain the thick secretory endometrium and inhibit FSH/LH
questions.answer: Maintain the thick secretory endometrium and inhibit FSH/LH
questions.explanation: Progesterone from the corpus luteum keeps the endometrium ready for implantation and suppresses further follicle development; its fall causes menstruation.
questions.commonMistake: Saying progesterone builds the lining — oestrogen rebuilds it; progesterone maintains and secretes it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: sperm are produced in the ________ and are kept at a temperature slightly below body temperature in the ________.
questions.explanation: The scrotum holds the testes outside the abdominal cavity, providing the cooler environment required for spermatogenesis.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the penis produces sperm — it is only the copulatory organ; production is in the testes.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: if fertilisation occurs, the implanted embryo secretes ________, which maintains the corpus luteum so that ________ continues to be produced and menstruation does not occur.
questions.explanation: hCG rescues the corpus luteum from degeneration; its progesterone keeps the endometrium intact through early pregnancy — and hCG is what pregnancy tests detect.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the embryo makes progesterone directly early on — the corpus luteum still makes it, supported by hCG.

questions.prompt: Describe the four phases of the menstrual cycle with the key hormonal events of each.
questions.answer: (1) Menstruation (days 1–5): with no pregnancy, the corpus luteum has degenerated, progesterone and oestrogen fall, and the endometrium breaks down and is shed. (2) Follicular phase (days 1–13): FSH from the pituitary stimulates several ovarian follicles to develop, one becoming dominant; the growing follicle secretes oestrogen which rebuilds and thickens the new endometrium. (3) Ovulation (about day 14): a surge of LH causes the mature follicle to rupture and release the secondary oocyte into the fallopian tube. (4) Luteal phase (days 15–28): the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum and secretes progesterone, which maintains the thick secretory endometrium ready for implantation and inhibits FSH and LH so no new follicle matures; if no implantation occurs the corpus luteum degenerates, hormone levels fall, and the cycle restarts.
questions.explanation: Each phase with its hormone event; the final fallback sentence shows understanding of why the cycle repeats.
questions.commonMistake: Describing phases without hormones — phase names alone typically earn only half the marks.

questions.prompt: Classify the following into their contraceptive method categories: condom, oral pill, vasectomy, spermicidal jelly, rhythm method. State one mechanism for each of two of them.
questions.answer: Categories: condom — barrier method; oral pill — hormonal method; vasectomy — surgical (permanent) method; spermicidal jelly — chemical method; rhythm method — natural method. Mechanisms: the condom physically blocks sperm from entering the vagina and additionally reduces exchange of bodily fluids, so it lowers STI transmission. The oral pill supplies oestrogen and progesterone, which inhibit the pituitary's FSH and LH secretion, so no follicle matures and ovulation does not occur. (Also: vasectomy cuts the vas deferens so semen contains no sperm; spermicides immobilise sperm at the cervix; the rhythm method avoids intercourse during the fertile window around ovulation.)
questions.explanation: Correct classification of all five plus two explicit mechanisms — the classification itself carries marks.
questions.commonMistake: Placing the condom in the 'chemical' category — it is a physical barrier; the jelly is the chemical one.

questions.prompt: Explain hormonal control of the menstrual cycle from day 1 to ovulation, then state what happens if fertilisation does occur.
questions.answer: At the start of the cycle (day 1) menstruation is under way because the previous cycle's corpus luteum has degenerated and progesterone and oestrogen have fallen, causing the endometrium to shed. The falling hormones release the pituitary from inhibition, so FSH rises and stimulates several follicles in the ovary to begin developing. During the follicular phase the dominant follicle grows and secretes increasing oestrogen, which stimulates regeneration and thickening of the endometrium. As oestrogen reaches a high level it triggers a surge of LH from the pituitary, and at about day 14 this LH surge causes the mature follicle to rupture and ovulation occurs, releasing the secondary oocyte into the fallopian tube. If fertilisation occurs in the tube, the dividing embryo reaches the uterus and implants in the endometrium; the embryo then secretes hCG, which maintains the corpus luteum so it keeps producing progesterone. Progesterone keeps the endometrium thick and vascular and inhibits FSH and LH, preventing further ovulation, so menstruation does not occur and pregnancy continues — at least until the placenta takes over progesterone production.
questions.explanation: A continuous hormonal narrative — falling hormones, FSH, oestrogen, LH surge, ovulation, then the hCG branch — is exactly the structure top answers use.
questions.commonMistake: Stopping at ovulation without the fertilisation branch — the question explicitly asks for both halves.

questions.prompt: A couple wishes to prevent pregnancy without hormones or surgery. Evaluate two suitable methods and explain why the condom is additionally recommended for reproductive health.
questions.answer: Two non-hormonal, non-surgical options: (1) the condom (barrier) — physically prevents sperm reaching the cervix, is reversible, needs no medical procedure, and its failure rate falls sharply with correct use; (2) the rhythm (safe period) method — intercourse is avoided during the fertile window (roughly days 10–17 of a regular 28-day cycle, centred on day-14 ovulation), requiring no devices at all. The condom is additionally recommended because it is the only method that reduces the transmission of sexually transmitted infections as well as preventing pregnancy: by enclosing the penis it blocks the exchange of semen and other bodily fluids through which HIV, gonorrhoea and other STIs spread. The rhythm method offers no infection protection, depends on accurate cycle prediction — irregular cycles or sperm survival up to five days make failure likely — and has a comparatively high failure rate, so a barrier method is preferred where STI risk exists.
questions.explanation: Two evaluated methods with mechanisms, then the condom's dual benefit and the rhythm method's limits — the evaluation structure earns the marks.
questions.commonMistake: Listing methods without evaluation — 'evaluate' requires strengths, limitations and the STI comparison.
